content.title: Promises: The Result Arrives Later
content.hook: In ordinary code, the next line usually runs after the previous line.
content.context:
Network work is different.

The browser may need to wait for another system.

That is why JavaScript uses a **Promise** to represent a value that is not ready yet.

A Promise can be understood as:

> “I will eventually give you a result, or tell you that this operation did not succeed.”
goals: Understand asynchronous timing, Promise fulfillment/rejection at a practical level, and the equivalent roles of `.then()` and `async`/`await`.

feedback.correct: The fetch work is asynchronous. The code continues to the next synchronous statement before the callback runs later.
feedback.incorrect: The fetch work is asynchronous. The code continues to the next synchronous statement before the callback runs later.

content.title: Why this matters
content.text:
Imagine a user clicks “Load profile.”

The request might take a little time.

If the program behaved as though the result already existed, it would make impossible assumptions.

Instead, the code needs a way to say:

> “When the data arrives, continue from here.”

`.then(...)` expresses that continuation.

content.title: The same idea with async and await

options.text: It lets this function continue at the correct point when the Promise resolves.
It converts JSON into HTML automatically.
It prevents all other JavaScript from running.

feedback.correct: `await` makes asynchronous code easier to read by keeping the sequence inside the async function.
feedback.incorrect: `await` makes asynchronous code easier to read by keeping the sequence inside the async function.

options.text: `getSecond()` is called only after `getFirst()` has produced its result.
Both are guaranteed to finish at exactly the same time.
Neither function can return a Promise.

feedback.correct: This code expresses a sequence: wait for the first result, then call the second operation.
feedback.incorrect: This code expresses a sequence: wait for the first result, then call the second operation.

content.title: Promise failure
content.text:
A Promise can also reject.

For practical reasoning, think of two outcomes:

**fulfilled → a result is available**

**rejected → the operation failed**

That means data-loading code needs a failure path.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** Asynchronous code is still a sequence. The difference is that some steps finish later.
**Senior habit:** When debugging async code, draw the timeline. Ask what has definitely happened, what is still waiting, and what can happen in between.
